Failed Role suggests a strong role-based or responsibility-based meaning of the trauma, but the rest of the profile does not indicate injury-related incapacity, inability to work, or family-protector themes that would support this appraisal. For this patient, it feels insufficiently grounded in the surrounding items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Permanent humiliation' is not impossible after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation and item set, which otherwise centers on fear-based post-collision threat, sensory reliving, and vulnerability rather than shame/humiliation. It is the least clinically integrated appraisal here and is hard to explain without other supporting shame-related items.

'Entrapment: Having no options' is not a clear contradiction, but for this trauma/profile it is weakly integrated compared with the other trigger items. The rest of the profile emphasizes crash reminders, reliving, danger appraisals, and hyperarousal. A strong entrapment trigger would usually be better supported by appraisals or memory content about being trapped or unable to escape, which are absent here.

vignette:
Robert had been the principal of Northwood High for twenty-two years, a man known for his steady presence and calm authority. That was before the accident. Now, six months after a cement truck ran a red light, he found himself sitting in a therapist's office, a stranger to himself. The collision had happened on a Tuesday afternoon, on his way home from work. He remembered the screech of tires, a horn blaring too late, and then an explosive, all-consuming roar as his world became a vortex of shattering glass and crushing metal. The last thing he saw before blacking out was the contorted face of a woman shouting for someone to call 911.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to stay in the past. It wasn't a memory he could recall so much as a film that would begin playing without his permission. Any loud, sudden noise—a dropped textbook in the library, a car backfiring in the parking lot—would trigger the entire sequence. The screech, the roar, the image of the other car appearing from nowhere, would flash behind his eyes with such visceral clarity that he would feel the phantom jolt of the impact in his bones, as if it were happening all over again. He found he could not put the core of the experience into words; the terror was a physical sensation, a pre-verbal horror that left him mute and trembling.

This constant reliving of the trauma fuelled a pervasive sense of threat. Robert, who once moved through the world with confidence, now saw danger everywhere. His conviction that catastrophe could strike at any moment meant he was constantly listening for it, and so the sounds of the high school—slamming lockers, shouting students—that were once background noise now felt like specific warnings directed at him. He became convinced that the world was an fundamentally unsafe place, a belief that poisoned every moment of peace. His certainty that he was permanently broken meant he was no longer safe, even in his own life; this belief kept his nervous system on a knife's edge, interpreting every unexpected event as the prelude to another catastrophe. He couldn't sleep, lying awake for hours listening for sounds of disaster. He was unable to relax, even in his own home, his body locked in a state of high alert. Because his body was already primed for disaster, any sudden sensory input—the roar of a truck passing outside, the high-pitched squeal of a student's sneakers in the hall—was immediately interpreted as a direct threat, bypassing rational thought entirely. This feeling of imminent danger made the memories more potent and frequent; the more threatened he felt, the more the film of the crash would play, creating a vicious feedback loop. The constant state of alarm also reinforced his worst fears about himself. He felt that this hypervigilance was proof that he had been permanently changed for the worse, that the capable man he once was had been destroyed in the wreckage.

These dark appraisals of himself and the world began to govern his life. The conviction that he was broken, that another man would have somehow avoided the accident, made him feel ashamed and weak. This belief that he had failed a fundamental test of survival kept forcing the memory of the crash to the forefront of his mind, as if his brain were searching the wreckage for the exact moment of his inadequacy. This belief system was the engine for his attempts to cope. He began to avoid going to work, the cacophony of a high school and the daily commute feeling like an insurmountable ordeal. His world began to shrink as a result; entire parts of town associated with his commute were now off-limits, and the sight of the school building from a distance, or even a yellow school bus on the road, became a fresh, potent reminder of what had happened and what he felt he had lost. At home, he would try to police his own mind, forcing himself to think only positive thoughts, a strategy that felt as effective as holding back the tide with a sieve. The sense of threat was too strong, and when it became unbearable, particularly at night, he would retreat to the kitchen and eat until a dull, physical discomfort could temporarily eclipse his psychological pain. He had learned that after being jolted awake by the memory of the impact, the act of eating—the focus on taste and texture, the growing feeling of fullness—was one of the few things that could ground him in the present and push the intrusive images away.

His strategies only tightened the knot. Calling in sick from the school he had dedicated his life to only served as concrete evidence for his belief that he was failing, that he was permanently damaged. This confirmation of his inadequacy would, in turn, amplify his sense of being under threat, making him even more sensitive to the triggers he was trying to avoid. His attempts to manage his distress were actively making him worse. He noticed that after a night of overeating, his shame would make him more jumpy the next day, and the slightest thing, like his wife taking longer than expected at the grocery store, would spiral into a certainty that something terrible had happened to her.

It was his wife, Mary, who finally insisted he seek help. She found him one afternoon staring out the window, having missed three days of work in a single week. He looked hollowed out, a ghost in his own home. Robert came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet resignation. He felt trapped in a cycle of fear he couldn't see a way out of. What he feared most was that his core belief was correct—that the man he used to be was gone for good, a casualty of that Tuesday afternoon.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not describe how Robert's negative beliefs (e.g., "I am broken") cause or intensify his sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not state that Robert's negative beliefs about himself or the world cause his intrusive memories to occur.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explain how Robert's negative beliefs make him more sensitive or hyper-aware of triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that the intrusive memories directly lead to Robert's use of maladaptive strategies like avoidance or overeating.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how Robert's pervasive sense of threat makes him more sensitive or reactive to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
